sachet_water_ldpe.impact_fact: Nigerians use about 13.7 million water sachets every day (NESREA figure), and empty sachets were named a major cause of Lagos floods. Pickers skip them because they are paid by weight!
preparation_steps: Shake out the water and let it dry.
Keep them in one bag (a rice bag works) until you have a bulk.
Best: hand them to a sachet scheme such as RecyclePoints.
No scheme near you? Pack them tightly into a bottle (eco-brick) or tie them in a bag for your PSP collector.
warnings: DON'T BURN: burning plastic gives off toxic fumes, and open burning of waste is an offence.
DON'T LITTER: sachets block drains and flood your street.
sachet_water_ldpe.legal_guidance: The law (NESREA S.I. 28 of 2009) lists 'water sachet' as litter: it must go in a bin, and occupants who let litter escape risk a ₦20,000 fine and/or 6 months. Sachets are NOT banned in Lagos.

pet_bottle.composition: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET, code 1). The cap is a different plastic.
pet_bottle.impact_fact: Nigeria uses about 150,000 tonnes of PET bottles a year, half of them in Lagos, and roughly 4 in 5 are never reused or recycled (FBRA, 2019). Recycling PET saves about 40% of the energy of making new!
pet_bottle.market_value: ₦250/kg (street collectors) up to about ₦600/kg for clean white PET (2025 reports; prices change)
preparation_steps: Empty it and give it a quick rinse.
Take off the cap and keep it separate.
Crush it flat, then bag it with other bottles.
Clear (white) bottles sell best.
warnings: Don't leave liquid inside: dirty bottles get rejected.
Don't throw bottles in gutters: they block drains.
pet_bottle.legal_guidance: Recyclables must be separated before collection (S.I. 28 of 2009, Reg 11), and drinks companies must run bottle buy-back schemes. PET bottles are NOT banned in Lagos.

battery.composition: Depends on type: lead and acid (car/inverter), lithium and flammable liquid (phone/power bank), zinc and manganese (AA/AAA).
battery.impact_fact: Over 55 million children in Sub-Saharan Africa have blood-lead levels above 10 µg/dL, linked to unsafe recycling of lead-acid batteries and e-waste. Never crack a battery open!
preparation_steps: Do NOT open or crush it.
Small batteries (AA, button, lithium): tape both ends with clear tape.
Keep in a dry plastic container away from heat and children.
Car/inverter battery: return it to the dealer. Others: e-waste centre or shop that takes old batteries (call first).
warnings: DON'T puncture, crush or open: fire and chemical risk.
DON'T bin or burn it: toxic metals, and burning waste is an offence (₦200,000 and/or 1 year).
Hot or swollen phone/power-bank battery: stop using it and keep it outdoors on a non-flammable surface.
battery.legal_guidance: Open burning of waste is an offence (S.I. 28 of 2009). Batteries are on Nigeria's producer take-back list, and e-waste rules (S.I. 23 of 2011) ban dumping or burning them.

aluminium_cans.composition: Aluminium alloy with a thin plastic lining inside.
aluminium_cans.impact_fact: Recycling aluminium saves about 95% of the energy needed to make new metal. Cans are cash: collect a bag and sell it by weight!
aluminium_cans.market_value: Changes weekly: ask the buyer for today's price per kg (the old ₦50-80/kg figure is outdated)
preparation_steps: Empty and rinse the can.
Crush it to save space (wear gloves).
Keep aerosol cans out of the bag.
Sell by weight to a scrap buyer or hand it to a recycler.
warnings: Sharp edges: wear gloves when crushing.
No aerosol cans in the cans bag (explosion risk).
aluminium_cans.legal_guidance: Cans and metals are on Nigeria's producer take-back list (S.I. 28 of 2009, Schedule VIII) and must be separated before collection.

food_waste.composition: Organic matter (starch, protein, fat) and water: rice, peels, bones, stew.
food_waste.impact_fact: Lagos makes about 11,000 tonnes of waste a day and roughly half is organic. Rotting food in dumps releases methane, which traps about 80 times more heat than CO2 over 20 years!
preparation_steps: Separate food from plastics, sachets and paper.
Use a bin with a lid or a tied bag, and empty it daily.
Home compost: mix scraps with dry leaves. Cooked food is better in a bokashi bin.
No compost? Tie it in a bag for your PSP collector.
warnings: Don't mix food waste with recyclables: it spoils them.
Don't burn it or dump it in drains: it attracts flies and rats.
food_waste.legal_guidance: Households must keep waste in lidded bins or tied bags and separate recyclables (S.I. 28 of 2009, Reg 11 and 13). The law recognises backyard composting of food waste.

glass_bottle.composition: Soda-lime glass (silica sand, soda ash, limestone).
glass_bottle.impact_fact: In May 2024 Beta Glass and Wecyclers launched cullet trucks in Lagos to collect old bottles and melt them into new ones. Your empty bottle can become a new bottle!
preparation_steps: Rinse the bottle or jar and remove the lid.
Deposit bottles (beer, soft drink): return them whole to the seller.
Wrap broken glass in thick paper, label it, and wear gloves.
Hand clean glass to Wecyclers or RecyclePoints (call first).
warnings: Broken glass cuts: wrap it and wear gloves.
Don't mix glass loose with other recyclables: it can hurt collectors.
glass_bottle.legal_guidance: Glass is on Nigeria's producer take-back list (S.I. 28 of 2009, Schedule VIII, from 2011) and recyclables must be separated before collection.

paper_cardboard.composition: Cellulose fibre (corrugated cardboard, newsprint, office paper).
paper_cardboard.impact_fact: Cartons are cash: collectors pay about ₦100/kg and resell at ₦180-230/kg. Nigeria's Dahua paper mill in Ogun turns waste paper from Lagos and other states into packaging!
paper_cardboard.market_value: About ₦100/kg for clean, dry cartons (collector price reported; varies)
preparation_steps: Keep paper and cartons dry and clean.
Flatten boxes and tie them in bundles.
Don't soak cartons to add weight: buyers reject them.
Greasy boxes and tissue go in the general bin.
warnings: Wet or greasy paper can't be recycled.
Don't burn paper: open burning of waste is an offence.
paper_cardboard.legal_guidance: Newsprint and paper are on Nigeria's producer take-back list (S.I. 28 of 2009, Schedule VIII), and recyclables must be separated before collection.

e_waste.composition: Plastics, copper, gold and other metals, plus lead, mercury and flame retardants.
e_waste.impact_fact: Africa formally collects and recycles less than 1% of its e-waste (Global E-waste Monitor 2024). Burning cables releases lead and mercury into your neighbourhood!
preparation_steps: Switch off and unplug; remove the battery if it comes out easily.
Reset the phone and wipe your data first.
Keep it whole: don't smash or burn it for the copper.
Take it to an approved e-waste centre (call first).
warnings: DON'T burn cables or break open devices: toxic fumes.
DON'T put e-waste in household bins or dumpsites: it is illegal.
Wipe your data before handing over.
e_waste.legal_guidance: E-waste must not be dumped, burned or binned; producers must take back old devices and consumers return them to collection points (S.I. 23 of 2011). Penalty for individuals: up to ₦200,000 and/or 6 months (2011 figure).
